paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, I've enjoyed another great day in interviews. I am so impressed with how well you're all growing in your teaching skills and your language skills. I've heard a few of you just in these last few days whose English has radically improved. I mean radical. I remember you on arrival day and here you are six, eight, ten months later and you're just talking to me like you're a native English speaker. So impressed.

I know that's hard work. I know you've gone through some serious hard work to make that happen and I just told you, I'm just totally impressed by it. I love you. You're looking great and I want to say that. I am impressed by how you're looking. I mean you look good. You look healthy. You look, your countenances are bright, bright as any of you've ever seen. I'm sure you're feeling this yourself. You're feeling the Lord's love for you as you're doing what's right.

One of the great American presidents, Abraham Lincoln once said, quote, "when I do good, I feel good and when I do bad, I feel bad," close quote. Now it really is about as simple as that. Abraham Lincoln probably didn't know exactly why he felt bad when he did bad and good when he did good, but I'm sure that you all know.

The clearest explanation of this is found like many things in the Book of Mormon. In Moroni chapter seven, starting in verse 12, Mormon explains in a letter to his son Moroni, quote, "Wherefore, all things which are good cometh of God; and that which is evil cometh of the devil; for the devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin, and to do that which is evil continually. But behold, that which is of God inviteth and enticeth to do good continually; wherefore, every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God," close quote.

A few verses later, Mormon goes on to explain how this is brought to us. How it happens. What's the mechanical function, if you will, that allows this to be true? He says this, starting in verse 16, quote, "For behold, the Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil; wherefore, I show unto you the way to judge; for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ; wherefore ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of God. But whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do evil, and believe not in Christ, and deny him, and serve not God, then ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of the devil; for after this manner doth the devil work, for he persuadeth no man to do good, no, not one; neither do his angels; neither do they who subject themselves unto him. And now, my brethren, seeing that ye know the light by which ye may judge, which light is the light of Christ, see that ye do not judge wrongfully; for with that same judgment which ye judge ye shall also be judged. For I beseech of you, brethren, that ye should search diligently in the light of Christ that ye may know good from evil; and if ye will lay hold upon every good thing, and condemn it not, ye certainly will be a child of Christ," close quote.

Now I am confident in saying that many of you are truly becoming more than ever before a child of Christ. Put that up from this quest you have taken up, because in the quest or the journey we actually find all the answers. Many people are mistaken when they believe that the answers come at the end of the journey. They don't. They come along the way and they usually come disguised as problems. And as we embrace the challenge of the problem, we learn the answer in the solution to the problem which will bless us for the rest of our lives. And we also learn about our own strengths and capacities.

There's an old proverb about a king whose people had grown soft and weak. The king had been such a great king that the kingdom had just prospered so dramatically that people had just gotten comfortable and weak and soft. The king was very dissatisfied with this condition, and so he hoped to teach his people a lesson. His plan was simple. He would place a large boulder in the middle of the main road, completely blocking entry into the city. He would then hide nearby and observe the people's reactions. How would they respond? Would they band together to remove the boulder? Or would they get discouraged, quit, and return home?

With growing disappointment, the king watched as person after person after person came to this obstacle, this challenge, this problem, the boulder, and just turned away. Or maybe they tried half-heartedly and then gave up. Many openly complained or cursed the king, or fortune, or bemoaned their sad state, or the inconvenience, or how much it was going to cost them to not be able to sell their goods in the city, or some other complaint. But none of them managed to do anything about the problem.

After several days, the king was about to give up, and then came along a lone peasant, a farmer. He was on his way into the city to sell his produce. When he got to the boulder, he didn't turn away. Instead, he put his shoulder to it, and he strained, and he strained, and he pushed, and he shoved, trying to get it out of the way, but he just wasn't strong enough. And then an idea came into his head.

He scrambled away into the nearby woods to find something he could use as a lever. Finally, he returned with a very large branch from a tree that he had crafted into this lever that he could stick under the boulder and dislodge it and push it out of the way from the road. Interestingly enough, in the story, beneath the rock were a purse of gold coins and a note from the king, which said, "The obstacle in the path becomes the path." Never forget, within every obstacle is an opportunity to improve our condition. That's the end of the story.

And so it is with us, dear sisters and elders. In the lockdown, we are learning many things about ourselves and how we want to be. Like Abraham Lincoln, we are learning that when we do bad, we feel bad. And when we do good, we feel good. We are learning that the better we do in following the light of Christ, the better we feel and the more good we can do. See every problem in your life as the very solution that you will need for your future growth and improvement.

Go forth in enthusiasm and confidence and challenge the problems. Look for ways to get around them. Never quit. Never give in. Never be willing to walk away because it's in the problem that you're going to find the answers that you will need to have in your life now and later on. As you do this with confidence and faith, the Lord will continue to bless you and continue to improve you.

You have our confidence and our love. We are so very proud of you. Keep being innovative, keep being proactive, keep being patient and kind and tolerant. Look at your Kabahays, your companions and see in them people who the Lord loves as much as he loves you. Recognize that they have problems just like you have problems. And recognize that as you see them, as the Lord sees them, you are exercising the spirit of discernment and the bond between you and those you serve with and live with will grow stronger and stronger, literally lasting a lifetime and beyond. We love you. Have a great night.
